news_drafts.headline: Vale of White Horse plans to use £3.6m of reserves in 2027/28 against a sustainable £2.9m
news_drafts.lead:
Vale of White Horse District Council's medium-term financial plan (MTFP) projects it will draw £3.6m from its reserves, the money it has put aside, in 2027/28. The sustainable level is £2.9m, leaving a shortfall of £754,000. The figures are in the budget-setting report going to the council's Cabinet on 9 October 2026.

The gap widens in later years, according to the plan the council agreed in February 2026. The shortfall against the sustainable level is projected at £2.1m in 2028/29, £3.3m in 2029/30 and £4.8m in 2030/31. The report says the amount expected to be used in 2027/28 "was much higher than that needed in 2026/27 and would not be in line with the recommended parameters, based on current estimates". Beyond that year, it says, use of reserves "was projected to continue to be unsustainable and outside of the parameters set".

The report says "action will be required by the council to address the increasing budget gap". It adds that the pause in local government reorganisation, the restructuring of councils in the area, means the council now has to deal with the gap sooner than it first expected.
news_drafts.paper_title: VALE Cabinet budget setting report Oct 2026

news_drafts.headline: Vale of White Horse: all eight key financial audits rated Substantial; cyber security rated Limited
news_drafts.lead:
All eight of the Vale of White Horse's key financial control audits for 2025/26 were completed with a "Substantial" assurance rating, the Joint Audit and Governance Committee was told on 6 October. The audits covered accounts payable, accounts receivable, council tax, the general ledger, business rates, treasury management (how the council borrows and invests its cash), payroll, and housing benefit and council tax reduction claims. Together they produced five management actions, all the lowest priority, and none rated Priority 1 or 2.

The internal audit and risk manager's overall opinion on 2024/25 was that there was "a satisfactory system of governance, risk, internal control", with enhancements recommended in some areas. One audit went the other way: cyber security, including artificial intelligence, was rated "Limited", which the papers say means significant improvement is needed. It produced nine management actions, two of them Priority 1 (fundamental to service integrity), five Priority 2 and two Priority 3.

The external auditor, Bishop Fleming, disclaimed the 2024/25 accounts for both councils, meaning it did not give an opinion on them, as part of wider problems across local audit. Its roadmap aims for qualified accounts for 2025/26 and unqualified for 2026/27, subject to satisfactory progress on "build back" work. The committee also said the number of overdue internal audit recommendations had been "excessive", and recent reports show it falling. Three audits were deferred from the 2025/26 plan: two pending the Ocella replacement project, and one moved to 2027/28.

news_drafts.headline: Vale of White Horse investment returns ahead of budget as deposit rates beat forecast
news_drafts.lead: The Vale of White Horse council expects to receive £1.146m more in investment income than budgeted for 2026–27, driven by higher returns on its treasury deposits, the cabinet heard this week. The council's cash reserves are earning 4.26 per cent on average, outperforming the government's Sterling Overnight Index Average benchmark of 3.74 per cent. However, the council is also forecasting a £698,000 overspend on employee costs in the first quarter, largely because of spending on staff for the local government reorganisation programme, project surveyors and temporary legal cover. A £0.7m underspend on disabled facilities grants, which fund home adaptations for disabled people, is under national review by the Department for Health and Social Care, and the council risks having to return unspent money.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E - Treasury Invest as at 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Vale holds £3m escalator-rate investment in Gravesham Borough Council
findings.detail: The investment schedule includes one escalator-rate deposit of £3m with Gravesham Borough Council maturing 17 May 2027. Escalator rates, which typically increase over the investment period, are unusual in local authority treasury operations; the table does not explain the commercial rationale for this structure. All other investments are either fixed-rate or call/variable-rate deposits.
findings.matters: Unusual deposit terms signal either higher perceived credit risk or special commercial arrangements; a lender assessing Vale's treasury risk management would want to understand the rationale and any implications for Vale's exposure to this counterparty.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E - Treasury Invest as at 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Vale holds two investments in Cornwall Council at 8.00% and 7.50%, substantially above the portfolio average rate
findings.detail: The schedule shows £5m invested in Cornwall Council at 8.00% due 17 April 2026 and £5m at 7.50% due 27 April 2026. These rates are notably higher than the bulk of the portfolio, which is deployed at 4.0 to 4.6% with peers such as Reading (4.06%), Leeds (4.10%), and North Tyneside (4.40%). Vale also holds £3m with Central Bedfordshire Council at 6.40% (16 April 2026), suggesting either credit risk premium on these counterparties or favorable market timing.
findings.matters: Finance directors at other councils benchmark their investment rates and counterparty spreads to assess market opportunity and credit risk; unusually high rates on specific counterparties flag either credit concerns or evidence of favorable deployment strategy.
findings.figures: 8.00%, 7.50% on Cornwall; 6.40% on Central Bedfordshire; portfolio average 4.0–4.6%

findings.paper_title: VALE Cabinet budget setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: If Local Government Reorganisation proceeds with April 2028 vesting as originally planned, capital projects may be subject to Secretary of State restrictions
findings.detail: If LGR vests on 1 April 2028 as originally intended, the Secretary of State may issue Section 24 directions that could restrict capital projects. The scope of these restrictions is unknown as the Secretary of State's discretion is very wide. The council cannot plan for specific restrictions at this stage.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand potential constraints on the council's capital spending that could affect asset maintenance and service delivery; this creates uncertainty around project completion and timing.
findings.quote: If that is the case, then capital projects may be subject to further restrictions which officers are unable to advise on at this time as the discretion of the Secretary of State is extremely wide in this regard.

findings.paper_title: VALE Cabinet budget setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: Three million pounds set aside in reserves for Local Government Reorganisation implementation, with allocation still being determined
findings.detail: The council has set aside £3.0m in reserves to cover transitional costs related to LGR implementation. The work to allocate these funds to specific purposes is ongoing. This reduces reserves available to support the revenue budget.
findings.matters: A material one-off provision drawn from reserves reduces the available buffer for future budget shortfalls and compounds the reserve sustainability challenge identified in the MTFP.
findings.quote: A provision of £3.0 million has been set aside in reserves and work continues to identify how these funds will be allocated.

findings.paper_title: VALE Cabinet budget setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: Managed vacancy factor of £250k cannot be achieved due to high staff retention, requiring review
findings.detail: The council budgeted for £250k in savings from managed vacancies (not filling vacancies to save money). However, staff retention has been higher than expected, preventing the council from achieving this saving. The factor will be reviewed.
findings.matters: If budgeted vacancy savings cannot be achieved, this indicates a structural overspend in payroll that must be addressed through other savings, service changes, or accepted as higher than planned costs.
findings.quote: the managed vacancy factor was reduced to £250,000, but we are still seeing a high level of staff retention which means the council has been unable to meet this level and therefore it will be reviewed further.
